scenes.heading: Histograms and stem-and-leaf plots
scenes.sub: Turn a long list of numbers into a picture
scenes.say: A long list of numbers is hard to read. Histograms and stem-and-leaf plots sort the numbers so you can see the answer at a glance.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Letters sorted into pigeonholes: A to E, F to J…
scenes.science: Values sorted into class intervals: 0 to 10, 10 to 20…
scenes.breaks: You can still read a letter in a pigeonhole, but a histogram bar hides the exact values.
scenes.say: Think of a school office sorting letters into pigeonholes, one for surnames A to E, one for F to J, and so on. A histogram sorts numbers into class intervals the same way, and each bar's height shows how full that interval is. But unlike letters, the exact values disappear inside the bar.

scenes.heading: Class intervals
points: Equal widths, e.g. 0 to less than 10, 10 to less than 20
A boundary value goes in the class it starts
Frequency = how many values in a class
scenes.say: First, group the data into class intervals of equal width, like zero to less than ten, then ten to less than twenty. A value on a boundary goes in the class that starts with it, so thirty goes in thirty to less than forty. The frequency is how many values land in each class.

scenes.heading: Reading a histogram
notes: Tallest bar = modal class, 160 to 165 cm
scenes.say: Here are the heights of thirty students. First the axes: height along the bottom as a number line, frequency up the side. Then the bars, which touch because the classes join with no gaps. The tallest bar, nine students, is over one hundred and sixty to one hundred and sixty-five centimetres. That's the modal class. Add every bar and you get thirty.
scenes.caption: Heights of 30 students. Height along the bottom, frequency up the side. The bars touch because the classes join. The tallest bar, 9 students, is over 160 to 165 cm: the modal class. Add every bar to get 30.

scenes.heading: Reading the histogram
scenes.question: How many of the 30 students are 165 cm or taller? What percentage is that?
scenes.say: How many students are one hundred and sixty-five centimetres or taller? Take the bars from one hundred and sixty-five upwards: eight, four and two. That's fourteen students. As a percentage, fourteen divided by thirty, times one hundred, is about forty-six point seven percent.
scenes.caption: How many are 165 cm or taller? The bars from 165 up are 8, 4 and 2: 14 students. 14 ÷ 30 × 100 ≈ 46.7%.

scenes.heading: Stem-and-leaf plots
points: Stem = tens digit, leaf = units digit
Order the leaves and always give a key
scenes.say: A stem-and-leaf plot splits each number into a stem, usually the tens digit, and a leaf, the units digit. Put the leaves in order and always write a key. Unlike a histogram, it keeps every original value. Squashed plot? Split each stem: leaves zero to four, then five to nine.

scenes.heading: A stem-and-leaf plot on its side
scenes.say: These fifteen game scores, from eighteen to fifty-two, made a stem-and-leaf plot with rows of one, four, six, three and one leaves. Turn the plot on its side and you get this histogram with classes of width ten.
scenes.caption: 15 game scores from 18 to 52 gave rows of 1, 4, 6, 3 and 1 leaves. On its side, the plot matches this histogram with classes of width 10.

points: Group data into equal class intervals
Start in, end out: 30 goes in 30 to 40
Histogram bars touch; tallest = modal class
Stem-and-leaf keeps every value — add a key
Check the frequencies add to the total
scenes.say: Quick recap. Group data into equal class intervals, remembering start in, end out. Histogram bars touch, and the tallest bar is the modal class. A stem-and-leaf plot keeps every value and needs a key. Always check your frequencies add to the total. Now try the practice questions!
